paras: The attempted lynching of Lemuel Cannon was a gathering of more than a hundred men and boys who surrounded the Minneapolis home of Cannon, a Black man accused of assaulting a young girl, on the evening of August 8, 1905, and organized a 'lynching party'. Cannon was in jail at the time, and most of the crowd went home after learning by telephone that he could not get bail. He was later indicted for criminal assault and tried in district court.

According to the Minneapolis Journal, it was alleged that a man approached a girl and a boy sitting on a bench in Farview park on Sunday night, August 6, claimed to be an officer, drove the boy off and forced the girl to submit by threatening her with arrest. The girl told her parents, the matter went to the police, and on August 8 Detective Tom Gallagher, Sergeant Ginsberg and Patrolman Hall arrested Cannon, whom the girl identified. The police said they had other incriminating evidence, and the paper described Cannon as an ex-convict who had served two penitentiary terms.

Word of the arrest spread through North and Northeast Minneapolis, and a party of young men met near Twentieth avenue N and set out for Cannon's home at 338 Quincy street NE, expecting him to be released on bail. The group grew as it crossed the river, telling bystanders its object, and two men in the center carried ropes obtained at a livery stable. Police officers who saw the crowd 'thought nothing of it because of the quiet and order', the Journal said.
The crowd waited near the house until one man telephoned Central station and learned that Cannon could not get bail. Most then went home, though a few stayed in case the report was wrong.

When Cannon was arraigned on August 9, several men from the crowd attended, and he was held for examination in $1,000 bail. One of them was quoted as saying, 'We will certainly get him if he is released on bail'. No arrests of anyone in the crowd are reported in the coverage.

The grand jury indicted Cannon for criminal assault, and at his arraignment on September 14 he was held without bail. By September 28 he was on trial before Judge F. C. Brooks; the court calendar of September 29 listed the charge as 'improper treatment of young girl'. No verdict appears in the coverage through the end of September.

The episode is known from a single local report in the Minneapolis Journal, headlined 'CROWD GATHERED TO LYNCH NEGRO' with the subhead 'ESCAPED VIOLENCE BECAUSE HE COULDN'T GET BAIL'. The Journal called the crowd 'Self-Appointed Avengers' who 'waited in vain', but it also wrote that they went 'quietly but determinedly to avenge the wrong', and it treated the accusation as established under the heading 'Cannon's Heinous Crime'. Its later items followed the prosecution, and on the trial's first day it ran a piece headlined 'HAS BAD RECORD' that listed his earlier convictions in St. Cloud and Duluth.
No other white paper and no Black newspaper reporting the crowd was found.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Lemuel Cannon
bases: A crowd of more than a hundred, carrying ropes, gathered at the accused man's home to lynch him and dispersed only when told he was held without bail (A1).

No one was killed: a crowd of more than a hundred organized a 'lynching party' with ropes under the pretext of avenging an alleged assault, but Cannon stayed in jail and the crowd went home (A1); it is a threatened or attempted lynching, not a completed one.
The crowd is reported only by the Minneapolis Journal of Aug. 9 (A1); later Journal items confirm the prosecution but not the crowd (A2, A3, A4).

accounts.label: Minneapolis Journal local report
accounts.gist: A crowd of more than a hundred, angered by the alleged assault, organized a lynching party with ropes and waited at Cannon's home, going home when told by phone that he could not get bail.

accounts.label: Police and prosecution account of the charge
accounts.gist: Police said the girl identified Cannon and that they had other incriminating evidence; the grand jury indicted him for criminal assault.

framing.detail: The Journal headlined 'CROWD GATHERED TO LYNCH NEGRO' and called the crowd 'Self-Appointed Avengers' who 'waited in vain', but presented the accusation as fact ('Cannon's Heinous Crime') and stressed his record ('HAS BAD RECORD').

versions.value: criminal assault / 'brutal assault on young girl'

conflicts.note: Wording differs between the news reports and the court calendar; both refer to the same case before Judge Brooks.
